subject: Biotechnology
title: The Discovery of DNA Structure
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Discovery of DNA Structure.

hook.text: In 1953, Watson and Crick built a model of DNA — revealing the double helix that stores all genetic information.

buildup.text: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray Photo 51 provided the crucial evidence — showing DNA's helical shape and dimensions.

discovery.text: The base-pairing rule — A with T, C with G — explained how DNA copies itself perfectly every time.

twist.text: Franklin died in 1958 and never received the Nobel Prize — her contribution went unrecognized for decades.

climax.text: The double helix gave biotech its foundation — once you know the structure, you can learn to manipulate it.

punchline.text: One photograph changed biology forever — and launched modern biotech.

quiz.question: Whose X-ray photograph was crucial to discovering DNA's structure?

details.summary: Watson and Crick determined DNA's double helix structure in 1953 using X-ray crystallography data from Rosalind Franklin and chemical rules from Erwin Chargaff. This discovery revealed how genetic information is stored and copied, launching modern molecular biology.
details.whyItMatters: The double helix discovery is one of the most important scientific breakthroughs in history. It explained how genes work, how traits are inherited, and opened the door to genetic engineering, genomics, and all of modern biotechnology.
takeaways: Watson and Crick proposed the double helix model of DNA in 1953
Franklin's X-ray data and Chargaff's base pairing rules were essential evidence
The structure explained both information storage and replication mechanisms

faq.question: What was Rosalind Franklin's contribution to the discovery?
faq.answer: Franklin produced Photo 51, an X-ray diffraction image of DNA that clearly revealed its helical structure and dimensions. Watson and Crick used this data, shown to them without Franklin's knowledge, to build their model. She received no Nobel recognition before her death in 1958.

faq.question: Why was determining DNA's structure so important?
faq.answer: The structure immediately suggested how DNA replicates: strands separate and each serves as a template. It revealed how information is encoded in base sequences and how mutations occur. Every advance in genetics and biotechnology traces back to this structural insight.
